chapter_title: Function Parameters and Return Values: Data Flow

screens.title: Function Parameters and Return Values
screens.subtitle: How data moves into and out of functions using parameters and return statements

narration.text: In this lesson we'll map the flow of data between calling code and functions. You will learn what parameters are, why C uses pass-by-value, how a function returns a result, and why local variables are isolated to their function. Think of a function as a small kitchen: you hand ingredients to it, the kitchen uses local copies of those ingredients, and it sends a finished dish back. That copy behavior—pass by value—prevents unexpected changes to the original ingredients in the main kitchen. We'll study example functions that add numbers, calculate areas, and convert temperatures, showing how arguments are copied and how return values are captured. We'll also highlight common errors: ignoring a function's return value, mismatched types that truncate data, and expecting internal modifications to change caller variables. By the end you should be able to write parameterised functions, choose the correct return type, and reason about variable scope. Start by noticing how a function's signature names the expected inputs and the type it promises to return. How will you use this pattern to keep your code clear and safe?

keyIdea.title: Core Idea
keyIdea.text: Parameters are local copies passed to functions (pass by value). Functions send results back with return; local variables live only during the function call.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Function Parameters and Return Values
Function Parameters and Return Values
Understanding how data is passed into functions and how results travel back to the caller.
In this lesson

Coming up
Step through code examples and diagnostics that show how values are copied, returned, and why scope matters for modular code.
Explore Key Topics
Pass by Value

Return Values

Visual Concept

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you'll gain from this chapter

narration.text: Over the next screens you'll practice four specific skills that make functions reliable and reusable. First, you'll learn to explain pass-by-value: what it means, why C copies argument values into parameters, and how that protects your caller's variables from unintended changes. I'll give a clear example so you can describe the mechanism in your own words. Second, you'll describe and use the return statement: choosing the right return type, returning a computed value, and making sure the caller stores that value so it isn't discarded. We'll demonstrate what happens when you ignore a return. Third, you'll write functions with multiple parameters and mixed data types, seeing how implicit conversions can promote or truncate values and how to avoid precision loss. Finally, you'll understand local variable scope: why locals live only during the function call, why they can't be accessed by the caller, and how that supports modular programming. Each objective includes a small mnemonic and a verified competency milestone to confirm you can apply these skills in real code. Are you ready to practice with real C examples?

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice and Pitfalls
screens.subtitle: Concrete outcomes and common mistakes to avoid

narration.text: These objectives focus on doing and recognizing mistakes. You'll write functions that accept parameters and return values, test them, and notice what goes wrong when types do not match or returns are ignored. For example, assigning a double return to an int can truncate decimals; we'll demonstrate this and show how to correct it by using matching types or explicit casting with intent. You'll also practice spotting a pass-by-value misconception: if a function appears to modify an argument but the caller's variable does not change, that is expected behavior in C. We will use small code exercises to confirm you can both read a function prototype and predict its effect, and to ensure you can choose void versus typed returns appropriately. Each objective has a short mnemonic to help recall the rule, and a milestone that verifies you can both explain and apply the concept in a short C program. After practice, you'll be able to reason about argument copying, return capture, and local variable lifetime with confidence. Which pitfall do you think causes the most real bugs in small programs?

screens.title: What Is a Parameter and What Is a Return Value?
screens.subtitle: Define the two directions of data flow between caller and function

narration.text: A parameter is a variable named in a function's signature that receives an argument value when the function is called. In practice, parameters let you write one function that operates on different inputs. The return value is the typed result a function sends back to the caller using the return statement. Together they form a data contract: the caller supplies inputs with a matching type, the function performs work using local copies of those inputs, and then it returns a result of the declared type. For example, a function declared to return an int must provide an integer via return. If no value is needed, the function is declared void and does not return data. A key real-world way to think about this is a vending machine: you insert coins (arguments), the machine processes them internally, and it dispenses a product or receipt (return value). One common misconception is to confuse parameters with the caller's variables; they are separate names bound to copies of the data at the moment of the call. Practice naming parameters clearly so the contract is obvious to callers. Can you state the contract for a function that takes two doubles and returns a double?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Parameters accept input values when a function is called; return values send results back to the caller via return.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Parameters and Return Values
Term definitions
Clear, concise definitions and a mnemonic to remember them.
Parameter (Argument)
A named local variable in a function that receives a copy of the caller's value at the time of the call.
Return Value
A typed value sent back to the caller with return. The caller must capture it to reuse the result; otherwise it is discarded.
Key Takeaway

Parameters form the input side of the contract; returns form the output. Treat them as separate names and separate storage.

Analogy: Vending Machine
Insert coins and choose a selection (caller provides arguments). Internal mechanisms use those inputs and dispense a product or receipt (the return value). Your coins outside the machine remain unchanged by internal processing.
Examples
Prototype: int addNumbers(int a, int b); — parameters a and b, return type int.
Prototype: void printHello(void); — no parameters, no return value.
Check your understanding
Write the contract for a function that converts Celsius to Fahrenheit: which parameter type and return type should you choose?

screens.title: Pass by Value — The Copying Process
screens.subtitle: Step through how arguments become separate parameter copies

narration.text: Pass by value means the caller's argument values are copied into parameters when the call is made. Step one: the caller evaluates expressions used as arguments. Step two: for each parameter, the compiler allocates a local slot and copies the argument value into that slot. Step three: the function body executes using those local slots; any assignments to the parameters modify only the local copies. Step four: when the function returns, its local variables are destroyed, leaving the caller's originals untouched. For instance, if main has int x = 10 and you call modify(x), the modify function receives a copy set to 10. If modify multiplies its parameter by two, only the local value changes; main's x remains 10 after the call. A common misconception is assuming the parameter is an alias to the caller's variable; in C it is not. This protects calling code from accidental side effects but means a function cannot change caller variables unless you explicitly use pointers. Understanding pass by value helps you reason about safety, predictability, and how to design APIs that either maintain immutability or deliberately modify external data using pointers in later chapters. How does this copy model change the way you design a function signature?

keyIdea.title: Pass by Value
keyIdea.text: Arguments are copied into parameters; functions modify copies, not the caller's variables, preserving caller state.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Pass by Value
Pass-by-value steps
A clear numbered process to reason about copying behavior.
1. Evaluate arguments
Compute the values used as arguments in the caller before the call begins.
2. Copy into parameters
Allocate local parameter slots and copy the evaluated values into them.
3. Execute function body
All modifications affect the local copies only; the original caller values are unchanged.
4. Return and destroy locals
Return sends a value back; local parameter slots are freed at function exit.
Key Takeaway

Pass by value isolates behavior and avoids accidental side effects, but it does not allow functions to modify caller variables directly.

Concrete Example
#include <stdio.h>

void modify(int v) {
  v = v * 2; // modifies local copy only
  printf("Inside modify, v = %d
", v);
}

int main() {
  int original = 10;
  modify(original);
  printf("After modify, original = %d
", original);
  return 0;
}
This prints 20 inside the function and 10 after, illustrating the copy behavior.

screens.title: addNumbers Example — Parameters and Return
screens.subtitle: Read and run the function that adds two integers and returns the sum

narration.text: Let's walk through a simple working example that demonstrates parameters, local variables, and return values. The addNumbers function is declared to take two ints and return an int. When main calls addNumbers(num1, num2), copies of num1 and num2 are passed into parameters a and b. Inside the function, a and b are local slots; the sum is computed and stored in result. The return statement sends result back to the caller where it can be assigned to sum in main. A common mistake is calling addNumbers without assigning the return: the function still runs but its result is discarded. Another subtle point is variable lifetime—result exists only during the function call, so it cannot be inspected from main. Walk through this code mentally: know which names exist in main and which exist in addNumbers. If you change a or b inside addNumbers, main's variables remain the same because of pass-by-value. Finally, check the prototype and definition types; they must match so the returned value is usable. Try predicting the printed output before running this code to confirm your model of copying and returning. What would happen if addNumbers were declared void?

keyIdea.title: Example insight
keyIdea.text: addNumbers shows parameters as local copies and return shipping the computed result back to the caller which must capture it.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › addNumbers Walkthrough
Code example
Study how arguments become parameters and how the return is used.
#include <stdio.h>

// Prototype: takes two integers, returns an integer
int addNumbers(int a, int b);

int main() {
  int num1 = 10;
  int num2 = 5;
  int sum;

  // Call addNumbers, passing copies of num1 and num2
  sum = addNumbers(num1, num2);

  printf("The sum of %d and %d is %d
", num1, num2, sum);
  return 0;
}

int addNumbers(int a, int b) {
  int result = a + b; // 'a' and 'b' are copies
  return result;      // Return the calculated sum
}
Takeaway
Assign the returned value to a variable if you need to reuse it; otherwise the result is lost.
Annotations
  • Prototype declares the expected parameter types and return type.
  • The call copies num1 and num2 into a and b.
  • result is local to addNumbers and cannot be accessed from main.
  • The returned int is stored in sum in main to preserve the value.
Check your understanding
Predict the program output and explain why num1 remains 10 after the call.

screens.title: Return Types and Void Functions
screens.subtitle: When to return a value and when to use void

narration.text: Choosing a function's return type defines how the caller can use the result. A typed function returns a value of that exact type; the caller typically assigns it to a variable or uses it in an expression. A void function does not return a usable value; it is appropriate when the function's job is to perform an action, such as printing to the console or updating global state. A frequent error is attempting to return a value from a void function or expecting a void function to provide data back. Another mistake is calling a function that returns a value and ignoring the result. Consider precision: returning a double and assigning it to an int will truncate the fractional part. This causes subtle bugs when you expect the full numeric result. Use the left-hand column of this comparison to prefer typed returns when the caller needs computed data, and use void when the operation is purely procedural. For example, calculateRectangleArea should return double to preserve decimal precision. When in doubt, return the most specific type that preserves the required information and clearly document whether the caller must capture the return.

keyIdea.title: Return vs Void
keyIdea.text: Return a value when the caller needs data; use void for procedures. Match receiving variables to return types to avoid truncation.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Return Types
Return vs Void
Decide whether your function should produce data or just perform an action.
Return a value
Use when the caller needs the computed result, e.g., calculating area or converting temperatures. Capture the returned value in the caller.
Use void
Use when the function performs a side effect only, such as printing or modifying global state. Do not expect data back.
Examples & Pitfalls
  • Returning double but storing in int truncates decimals — be explicit about types.
  • A void function cannot produce a result; attempting to return a value violates the declaration.
  • Calling a non-void function without capturing the return discards the value.
Key Takeaway
Match return types to the information the caller needs and always capture important results.

screens.title: Local Variables and Variable Scope
screens.subtitle: Why locals exist only during a function's execution

narration.text: Local variables are those declared inside a function and are allocated for the life of that function call. They are created when execution reaches their declaration and destroyed when the function returns. This limited scope means they can't be accessed from other functions or the caller. For example, result inside addNumbers exists only during addNumbers' execution; main cannot read it directly. This isolation helps keep functions modular and prevents accidental interference between different parts of a program. A common misunderstanding is assuming a local variable's value persists across calls; it does not, unless declared static, which is a different mechanism and outside this chapter's scope. Another point is that parameters themselves are local variables initialized with copies of the caller's arguments. Design your functions expecting that all locals are ephemeral: return any needed data explicitly. Finally, when debugging, remember that printing a local inside a function will show that value only while the function runs. How does this lifecycle influence your choice to return values rather than rely on side effects? Local Variables and Variable Scope means locals exist only during the function call; return values are needed to transfer computed information back to the caller.. In practical terms, why locals exist only during a function's execution. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Local Scope
keyIdea.text: Locals exist only during the function call; return values are needed to transfer computed information back to the caller.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Local Variables
Variable scope and lifetime
Understand why locals are destroyed at function exit and the implications for program design.
Why scope matters
Isolation prevents accidental modification and supports modular reasoning. Return values transfer only the needed data back to the caller.
Key Takeaway
Do not rely on local variables to persist beyond the function call; return values or use other mechanisms when persistence is required.
Example diagnostic
If you print a local inside the function you will see its current value. After the function ends, the local no longer exists and cannot be accessed or inspected from the caller.
Check your understanding
Explain why the variable result in a function cannot be printed from main without returning it first.

screens.title: calculateRectangleArea — Types and Precision
screens.subtitle: How parameter types affect returned results and precision

narration.text: This example demonstrates how choosing parameter and return types matters. calculateRectangleArea is declared to take two doubles and return a double. Passing floating-point values preserves fractional dimensions and the returned area retains decimals. If you instead declared parameters or the return type as int, you would lose fractional information. For example, passing 10.5 and 7.2 into a function declared to accept ints would truncate the inputs before the computation, producing an incorrect area. The recommended practice is to select the type broad enough to hold required precision. Also ensure the receiving variable in the caller matches the return type; assigning a double return to an int in main will truncate the decimal part and often hide subtle bugs. This screen reinforces the idea: the function's signature is a contract about data shapes. Predict the output of the example before running it and notice where precision would be lost if the types were changed. How will you choose types for geometric computations in your programs? calculateRectangleArea — Types and Precision means use parameter and return types that preserve precision. passing doubles and returning a double preserves fractional results for calculations like area.. In practical terms, how parameter types affect returned results and precision. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Type and Precision
keyIdea.text: Use parameter and return types that preserve precision. Passing doubles and returning a double preserves fractional results for calculations like area.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Rectangle Area
calculateRectangleArea example
Observe the types to avoid truncation.
#include <stdio.h>

// Prototype: takes two doubles (length, width), returns a double (area)
double calculateRectangleArea(double length, double width);

int main() {
  double rectLength = 10.5;
  double rectWidth = 7.2;
  double area;

  area = calculateRectangleArea(rectLength, rectWidth);
  printf("The area of a rectangle with length %.2f and width %.2f is %.2f
",
         rectLength, rectWidth, area);
  return 0;
}

// Definition
double calculateRectangleArea(double length, double width) {
  return length * width;
}
Notes
  • Parameters are doubles, preserving fractional input values.
  • The returned double keeps decimal precision for area calculations.
  • If you stored the return in an int, fractional data would be lost.
Key Takeaway
Match parameter and return types to the precision your computation requires; document the contract in the prototype.

screens.title: Common Mistakes with Parameters and Returns
screens.subtitle: Practical debugging tips for the most frequent errors

narration.text: Let's examine the common mistakes students make when working with parameters and return values. First, ignoring the return: calling a function that returns a value without assigning or using it wastes the computation. The function runs but the result is lost. Second, type mismatches: assigning a double return to an int truncates decimals and causes precision loss. Third, expecting pass-by-value to update caller variables: because C copies values into parameters, modifications inside the function do not affect the caller. Fourth, returning a value that doesn't match the declared return type leads to compilation errors or unexpected behavior. When debugging, check the function prototype, the call site, and how the result is stored. Use print statements to confirm where values change: print inside the function to see local values and print after the call to ensure the caller's variables are as expected. Finally, if you need to change caller variables, you will use pointers or references later, but for now recognizing pass-by-value clarifies why variables remain unchanged. Which of these mistakes have you encountered before and how did you fix it?

keyIdea.title: Mistakes to watch
keyIdea.text: Don't ignore return values, avoid type truncation, and remember pass-by-value does not mutate caller variables.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Common Mistakes
Ignoring return values
If a function returns data and you don't store or use it, the result is discarded. Assign important results to preserve them.
Type mismatch and truncation
Assigning a double return to an int truncates decimals. Match types or cast explicitly with awareness of possible data loss.
Pass-by-value expectation
Expecting a parameter change to alter the caller's variable is a logical error in C's pass-by-value model.
Debugging checklist
  1. Verify function prototype and definition types match.
  2. Ensure the caller captures the return value when needed.
  3. Use prints inside and outside the function to observe which variables change.
Key Takeaway
Follow a checklist: prototype, capture return, print to observe, and reason about pass-by-value.

screens.title: From Call to Return — Tracing Execution
screens.subtitle: Trace the lifecycle of values across a function call

narration.text: Tracing execution helps you predict program behavior. Begin with variables in main holding initial values. When main calls a function, imagine snapshots: first snapshot is main's memory before the call; second snapshot is the function at entry with parameter copies; third snapshot is during function execution where locals and parameters may change; final snapshot is after return where the caller receives the returned value and function locals are destroyed. Apply this to the earlier addNumbers example: snapshot one shows num1 as ten and num2 as five; snapshot two shows a and b set to those values; snapshot three shows result computed to fifteen; snapshot four shows sum assigned to fifteen in main while a, b, and result are gone. Use this mental model when debugging, placing print statements at key points to confirm snapshots. When types differ, also trace conversions: note whether promotions or truncation occur during the copy step. Doing this systematically will make it easier to find where a value diverges from expectation. As you trace calls, ask: at which snapshot should the value have changed, and did it?

keyIdea.title: Trace Execution
keyIdea.text: Visualize snapshots: before call (caller), at entry (parameter copies), during function (locals), and after return (caller receives result).

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Trace Execution
Snapshots across a call
Use a four-snapshot trace to track where values live and when they change.
Snapshot 1 — Before call: caller variables hold original values.
Snapshot 2 — At function entry: parameters are local copies initialized from caller values.
Snapshot 3 — During execution: parameters and other locals may change, but changes are local.
Snapshot 4 — After return: the caller receives the returned value and function locals are freed.
Practice
Apply this trace to an example call and use prints to confirm each snapshot in actual runs.
Quick checklist
  • Identify parameter copies at entry.
  • Note any conversions during copying.
  • Confirm returned value is assigned by caller.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.subtitle: Three essential ideas from this chapter

narration.text: Let's consolidate the most important ideas. First: Parameter (Argument) — a value passed to a function so the function can operate on that data; think of it as the input to a small, self-contained routine. Second: Pass by Value — C copies each argument's value into the function's parameter slots. Modifying parameters affects only those local copies, not the caller's variables. Third: Return Value — functions send results back to the caller using return; the caller must capture this returned value to use it. These three concepts are the backbone of safe, modular functions: clear inputs, internal processing on copies, and explicit outputs. Keep these in mind when you design function prototypes and when you debug unexpected behavior. Which of these will you check first when a function behaves unexpectedly?

keyIdea.title: Summary
keyIdea.text: Parameters are inputs, pass-by-value creates local copies, and return sends outputs back; capture returns to preserve results.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Key Concepts
Parameter (Argument)
A named input that allows the function to operate on specific data.
Pass by Value
Arguments are copied into parameters; internal changes do not affect the caller.
Return Value
A typed value sent back; the caller must capture it to reuse the result.
Takeaway
Treat function signatures as contracts: inputs, local processing, and explicit outputs. This model helps prevent bugs and clarifies ownership of data.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 2
screens.subtitle: Practical rules and a final checklist

narration.text: Finish with a short checklist you can apply immediately. First, always match the function's declared parameter and return types with the values you pass and receive to avoid implicit truncation or promotion. Second, when you need the result of a computation, capture the return value in the caller; otherwise the value is lost. Third, remember the lifecycle: parameters and locals exist only during the call; return any information the caller needs. Use prints at entry and after return to observe snapshots and find where values diverge from expectation. These practical rules will reduce common bugs and make your functions predictable and reusable. Try applying this checklist next time you write a small function: check types, check capture of return, and check the scope of variables. Which checklist item will you apply first in your next program?

keyIdea.title: Practical Rules
keyIdea.text: Match types, capture returns, and track variable lifecycles to prevent common function-related bugs.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Final Checklist
1. Match types
Ensure parameters and return types preserve required precision and semantics.
2. Capture return
Assign returned values when you need them; otherwise the result is discarded.
3. Track scope
Remember locals and parameters are temporary and exist only during the function call.
Final Takeaway
Use clear function contracts and the snapshot trace to reason about data flow and avoid surprises when functions interact.
